overview:
Photography is the art, science, and practice of creating images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation. It emerged in the early 19th century with the invention of light‑sensitive materials and has since evolved into a diverse field encompassing artistic expression, documentation, scientific analysis, and personal communication. Early photographic processes, such as the daguerreotype and calotype, required long exposure times and produced singular, fragile images. Over time, advances in chemistry, optics, and mechanical engineering enabled faster exposures, reproducible negatives, and portable cameras.

By the 20th century, photography had become widely accessible through roll film, compact cameras, and later digital sensors. Digital photography transformed the medium by replacing chemical processes with electronic image capture, enabling instant review, editing, and distribution. Today, photography spans numerous genres—portraiture, landscape, documentary, scientific imaging, commercial work, and more. It plays a central role in journalism, cultural memory, artistic innovation, and everyday communication through smartphones and social media.

Although photography is not a traditional subject of Jain canonical literature, Jain communities have engaged with photography in modern times for documentation of manuscripts, preservation of temple art, and recording of cultural heritage. In these contexts, photography serves as a tool for conservation, education, and historical study rather than a subject of religious doctrine.

primary_sources.title: No direct primary Jain text on photography
primary_sources.author: N/A
primary_sources.notes: Photography is a modern technological development and does not appear in classical Jain scriptures such as the Āgamas or Digambara canonical works. Jain institutions sometimes use photography for documentation and preservation, but this is a contemporary practice rather than a scriptural topic.

misconceptions.myth: Photography is purely a modern hobby without serious applications.
misconceptions.reality: Photography is used in scientific research, medicine, journalism, cultural preservation, and legal documentation, making it a vital tool across many fields.

misconceptions.myth: Digital photography completely replaced film photography.
misconceptions.reality: While digital photography dominates everyday use, film photography remains active in artistic, archival, and specialized professional contexts.

misconceptions.myth: A good camera automatically produces good photographs.
misconceptions.reality: Composition, lighting, timing, and the photographer’s skill are far more important than equipment alone.
